title: UAE Quits OPEC and OPEC+ as Hormuz Blockade Exposes Cracks in Saudi-Led Cartel
subhead: The UAE announced it will leave both OPEC and the wider OPEC+ alliance, removing roughly 13% of the group's production capacity and stripping Riyadh of its most capable spare-capacity partner. The timing, amid the Hormuz blockade, makes the split a structural blow delivered in the middle of the worst oil shock since the 1970s.

sections.heading: UAE Exit: A Cartel Loses Its Second Engine
sections.body:
The UAE will withdraw from both OPEC and OPEC+, its state news agency WAM announced, a move it framed as aligning with 'long-term strategic and economic vision' and 'national interest.' Abu Dhabi has been a member since 1967 and, pre-war, was the fourth-largest producer in the 22-member OPEC+ bloc behind Saudi Arabia, Russia and Iraq (TRT World, DW).

The numbers matter. Energy Minister Suhail Al Mazrouei told the New York Times that 'the world needs more energy... the UAE wanted to be unconstrained by any groups.' The country produces roughly 3.2-3.6 million bpd under quotas but holds spare capacity near 4.8 million bpd, with plans to push toward 5 million bpd (Reuters, via DW). MEES managing editor Jamie Ingram, citing IEA data, put the loss at 13% of OPEC's production capacity (TRT World).

Sources conflict on the exit date: TRT World reported the UAE said it would pull out 'on Friday,' while DW reported the departure takes effect May 1. Both agree the split is final.
sections.whyItMatters: Saudi Arabia can no longer share the burden of output cuts with a low-cost producer of UAE's scale. Defending prices becomes more expensive for Riyadh and its ability to discipline the wider group weakens — a change that will shape the market long after the Hormuz crisis resolves.

sections.heading: Why Now: Redirection, Not New Supply
sections.body:
The immediate market reaction was muted because Hormuz, not OPEC quotas, is setting prices. The UAE is redirecting about 1.8 million bpd to its Fujairah port on the Gulf of Oman coast via a pipeline running at maximum capacity (DW). Any new barrels cannot reach buyers while the strait stays blocked.

Analysts are split on near-term effect but not on direction. Rystad Energy's Jorge Leon said the exit 'takes a real tool out of the group's hands' and pointed to 'a potentially more volatile oil market as OPEC's capacity to smooth supply imbalances diminishes' (DW, TRT World). Brown University's Jeff Colgan told DW the exit is 'kind of a minor thing' short-term because Hormuz 'dominates the whole global oil picture' — but once normal, the UAE could add several hundred thousand extra barrels per day.

Capital Economics' David Oxley called it 'the thin end of the wedge,' warning that 'the ties binding OPEC members together have loosened.' OPEC once controlled more than half of global supply; it now commands less than a third (DW).
sections.whyItMatters: The UAE is betting it can monetise its spare capacity once the strait reopens, and in a market nearing demand peak, waiting inside a quota system looks like lost revenue. That logic, if copied, erodes the cartel from within.

sections.heading: Hormuz: Trump Rejects Iran's Seven-Day Offer
sections.body:
Brent traded at $107.29 a barrel, up 2.84% on the day and nearly 60% year on year, according to TradingEconomics data cited by FinanceFeeds. WTI was back above $94. Flows through Hormuz stand at about 33.7 million barrels a week — a fraction of pre-war traffic.

President Donald Trump rejected Iran's 22 September offer to reopen the strait within seven days, telling reporters 'I reject their proposal' and that Tehran had 'overplayed their hand' (CBS News, Axios, via FinanceFeeds). The Iranian offer had tied reopening to an end to the US naval blockade of Iranian ports, the release of frozen assets and an end to what Tehran calls US 'acts of aggression.'

Qatar has been acting as mediator, with the emir urging diplomacy as the Gulf faces a 'dangerous phase.' Qatar said Iran-Oman talks on Hormuz reached an 'advanced stage' (Anadolu Agency). Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Tehran is 'fully prepared for the war to be resumed' while remaining 'ready for diplomacy.' The Wall Street Journal reported Trump has told aides he sees renewed strikes as likely after the 3 November midterms.
sections.whyItMatters: The rejection removed the cheapest off-ramp the market had been pricing. With the midterm calendar now the key variable, oil is trading a grind with a dated risk attached: a real deal pushes Brent toward the mid-$90s, resumed strikes open the $120 case.

sections.heading: Rare Earths: The 10 November Deadline Looms
sections.body:
Market participants are focused on 10 November 2026, when China's rare earth export controls are due to be reintroduced if the current suspension is not extended. Under China's Announcement No. 61, licensing requirements could apply to foreign-made products containing Chinese-origin rare earths above certain thresholds, and to goods made using covered Chinese rare earth technology (Fastmarkets).

The effects of China's April 2025 heavy-rare-earth controls already show in prices. Fastmarkets assessed dysprosium oxide in Europe at $1,250-1,675/kg on 27 August versus $270-330/kg fob China — a roughly 4.9x divergence. Terbium oxide traded at $4,200-5,000/kg in Rotterdam versus $1,180-1,270/kg fob China, about 3.8x. No dysprosium or terbium oxide has been exported to Japan, the largest ex-China consumer, in 2026, per Chinese customs data.

The divergence has boosted non-Chinese producers: Australia's Lynas Rare Earths says it benefited from the controls, having started dysprosium oxide production in May 2025 and terbium oxide in June 2025. This comes as Trump officials publicly warn Beijing is 'weaponizing rare-earth dominance' and USA Rare Earth breaks ground on a $1.2 billion South Carolina facility.
sections.whyItMatters: If the November controls take effect as written, licensing reaches into separation equipment, strip-alloy production and magnet manufacturing — pulling supply chains well beyond raw materials. Ex-China price premiums tell you the market is already pricing that risk.

sections.heading: Russia Cuts Gas Forecasts as Europe Closes the Door
sections.body:
Russia has cut its 2026 natural gas output and export forecasts, a Reuters exclusive reported, as the EU moves toward ending purchases of Russian gas. The revision reflects a shrinking addressable market rather than a production failure: Moscow is writing down volumes it no longer expects to sell into Europe.

The context is a tightening European market. The EU Energy Commissioner Dan Jorgensen wrote to energy ministers warning of a 'price crisis linking to a supply crisis,' according to a letter seen by Bloomberg. European gas prices have more than doubled since the start of the US-led war on Iran in late February, hitting their highest level since late 2022 earlier this month.

EU gas storage was just over 70% full versus a seasonal norm of 86%, as high near-term prices made summer injections uneconomic. Jorgensen suggested governments could use flexibility under EU storage rules to lower the filling target to 80% and urged demand cuts where needed.
sections.whyItMatters: Russia is conceding its European gas market is gone while Brussels admits its buffer is thin. That combination means Asia will compete harder for LNG cargoes this winter, keeping upward pressure on prices even if oil stabilises.

sections.heading: China's Reserve Drawdown: Shock Absorber or Position Building
sections.body:
Chinese crude oil imports fell 20% year on year in April, 29% in May and 41% in June, according to customs data cited by the state-run Global Times. Beijing frames this as a deliberate buffer: by slowing purchases into the Hormuz crisis, China broke the 'panic buying driving prices higher' cycle and prevented the price spike from spilling into global inflation.

The claim is echoed elsewhere. Reports describe China cutting oil imports by as much as 32-40% during the Iran war and cushioning the shock by draining reserves, with one outlet noting the US has China to 'thank' for keeping oil prices from rising further.

Beijing rejects the framing that its reserves are 'leverage' or a 'weapon,' arguing that a flexible import posture is its most basic contribution to global stability — while also noting that EV adoption, solar and wind deployment have reduced its fossil dependence and given it more demand-side flexibility.
sections.whyItMatters: Regardless of the spin, the data shows a single buyer can materially move the global oil price by adjusting its purchasing pace. That gives Beijing a market lever it did not have a decade ago — useful precisely when others are squeezed.

bottomLine: The UAE's exit from OPEC and OPEC+ is the day's real news: it removes about 13% of the cartel's capacity, forces Saudi Arabia to carry price defence alone, and signals that producers are positioning for a post-Hormuz world rather than waiting out the crisis. On the strait itself, Trump's rejection of Iran's seven-day reopening offer pushed Brent to $107 and moved the timeline to the post-midterm window. Meanwhile the slow-burn stories kept building — China's rare earth controls return on 10 November, Russia is writing down its European gas market, and EU storage sits at 70% heading into winter. The common thread is not a single chokepoint but a widening set of actors deciding they can act unilaterally, whether Abu Dhabi on quotas, Beijing on minerals, or Tehran on a strait.
sources: DW, TRT World, Anadolu Agency, Reuters (via DW and headline reports), Fastmarkets, FinanceFeeds, Bloomberg (via Investing.com/Yahoo), Global Times, Gulf News, Upstream Online, Alhurra, CBS News, Axios, Wall Street Journal (via FinanceFeeds)
